title: LightWSP: Whole-System Persistence on the Cheap
problem: Existing whole-system persistence approaches either introduce high hardware cost or cause significant performance overhead. Prior WSP implementations require intrusive memory controller speculation mechanisms to handle multiple memory controllers.
motivation: Whole-system persistence provides transparency and performance benefits while enabling DRAM as LLC without burdening users with complex persistent programming.
method: The compiler splits the program into chunks called epochs (recoverable sections of code). At the end of each epoch, it saves key register values that the next chunk will need. The hardware then repurposes an existing battery-backed buffer called the write pending queue (which normally holds memory writes waiting to be sent to storage) as a log of changes. At each epoch boundary, it sends all the collected memory writes together to permanent storage, so the data survives a crash.
key_novelty: The core idea is repurposing an existing piece of hardware—the battery-backed write pending queue—as a change log, so the system can recover from crashes using minimal added hardware (0.5 bytes per core) and without needing to predict how multiple memory controllers will behave.
contributions: Compiler/architecture co-design for lightweight whole-system persistence
Novel use of battery-backed WPQ as redo buffer enabling crash-consistent persistence
Multi-controller support without costly speculation/misspeculation handling mechanisms
9% average runtime overhead with near-zero hardware cost per core
baselines: prior WSP with memory controller speculation
primary_theme: Lightweight WSP via WPQ redo buffering
